newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICAN TAX COMMISSION TACKLES BENEFIT FUNDS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICAN TAX COMMISSION TACKLES BENEFIT FUNDS.

text.p: South Africa's Katz Commission on Taxation on Thursday recommended a wide range of measures to crack down on the use of benefit funds to dodge tax.

The commission said in its sixth report that it was particularly concerned about the way in which benefit funds could be used to set up salary sacrifice schemes and tax shelters while rules on deductions had to be tightened up.
Salary sacrifice schemes involve employees accepting lower salaries but then expecting employers to pay contributions to benefit funds in return.
"The employee gets fund membership without having to purchase it out of after-tax income, and at no net cost to the employer," the commission said.
This only benefited high income earners and not low income earners and the self-employed, it said.
The commission said that in the case of registered medical schemes, the ability of employers to claim deductions for such contributions should be limited to a "rand for rand" basis.
This meant that for every rand contributed by employees, the employer could contribute another rand and claim it as a tax deduction.
Self-employed people should be able to deduct 50 percent of their contributions and employer contributions that were higher than approved limits should be taxed as income.
In the case of medical savings accounts, tax should be imposed on interest and cash withdrawals for non-medical purposes, the commission said.
Bonuses paid to reward medical scheme members for no or low claims should also be taxed.

The commission recommended that investments in so-called friendly societies, or mutual organisations, and registered medical schemes should remain untaxed because they were not large enough to provide significant tax shelters.

To prevent friendly societies from being used for salary sacrifice schemes, the commission said that "after a reasonable period of notice, employer contributions (should) no longer be tax deductable".

It recommended that the growth of schemes in friendly societies to fund education should be carefully monitored to insure that they were not being used by high income earners not usually associated with such schemes.
The special tax privileges available to the plethora of other benefit funds in South Africa should be withdrawn, the commission said.

These range from funds offering unemployment benefits to those covering disability. They would have to either continue operating without their special tax privileges, wind themselves up or register as pension funds, medical schemes or friendly societies.
"The balance will no doubt seek registration as either short or long term insurers," the commission said.
